title: Governance, Compliance and Medical Device Security

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: The AI Enablement Audit in Healthcare
children.blurb: An AI enablement audit in healthcare is a structured review of how a clinical or operational setting prepares for, deploys, and monitors artificial intelligence systems.

children.name: Local Models for Patient Data
children.blurb: Local models for patient data are AI systems that run inference and often training or fine-tuning within a healthcare organization's own infrastructure, rather than sending protected health information to external cloud services.

children.name: Software as a Medical Device
children.blurb: Software as a Medical Device covers software intended for medical purposes without being part of a physical device.

children.name: Bias in Clinical Triage
children.blurb: Bias in clinical triage refers to systematic differences in how an AI system assigns urgency, acuity, or priority to patients based on characteristics such as race, sex, age, language, insurance status, or disability.

children.name: Security of Connected Medical Devices
children.blurb: Security of connected medical devices covers the protection of networked clinical hardware, from infusion pumps and patient monitors to imaging systems and implantable devices, against unauthorized access, data interception, and manipulation.

sections.body: This field covers how hospitals and clinics check that an AI system is safe to use, how patient records stay private when models run locally, how regulators clear software as a medical device, how triage tools can treat some groups unfairly, and how networked devices like infusion pumps and monitors are protected. Artificial intelligence is now doing concrete work in each area: audits compare a model's outputs against written policies and clinical guidelines, local models run on hospital servers so patient data never leaves the building, cleared software goes through a formal review process before it can be sold for diagnosis or treatment, bias testing measures whether a triage tool gives different recommendations by race, sex, age or insurance status, and security scans look for open ports and weak credentials on connected devices. The site tracks 1000 medical AI models and 732 AI tools, which gives a sense of how many systems now need this kind of oversight. None of this is hypothetical; these are live systems in use or under review.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The work is uneven. Enablement audits are becoming common in large health systems, but there is no single accepted standard, so two hospitals can audit the same model and reach different conclusions. Local models for patient data are technically feasible and used in some radiology and pathology departments, but they require more in house computing skill than many smaller clinics have. Software as a medical device clearance is well defined in some countries, yet the rules were written before large language models, so many newer AI tools fall into gray areas. Bias in clinical triage is documented in published studies, but fixing it is hard because the bias often comes from historical referral patterns and missing data rather than the model itself. Security of connected medical devices remains a serious weak point, with many older devices still running unsupported operating systems and no easy way to patch them. The site tracks 6 active product liability and wrongful death lawsuits against AI companies and 210 compliance and regulation pages, which shows both the real consequences of failure and the gap between guidance and enforcement, but no audit can catch every failure and clearance does not guarantee a model works well on every patient.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader looking for a structured way to check a model before deployment would start with The AI Enablement Audit in Healthcare, which walks through the questions a hospital should ask about data, performance and oversight. Local Models for Patient Data explains the technical options for keeping records on site and the trade offs in speed, cost and maintenance. Software as a Medical Device covers the regulatory path for tools that diagnose or treat, including what counts as a device and what evidence is needed. Bias in Clinical Triage focuses on a specific high risk use, showing how triage scores can differ across groups and how to test for that. Security of Connected Medical Devices addresses the network side, from infusion pumps to imaging machines, and what hospitals can realistically do when a vendor stops supporting a device. Together these pages move from before deployment, through data handling and regulation, to specific risks in triage and device security, so a reader can follow one thread or use each page as a standalone reference.
